Finally, let us speak plainly about governmental stability — not as a conservative value or a liberal value, but as an American value.

We live in a world of authoritarian competitors who watch our internal divisions with unconcealed satisfaction. Every time our government is thrown into a constitutional crisis by a politically motivated impeachment proceeding, every time our senior officials spend months consumed by removal proceedings rather than governing, every time the world watches American democracy convulse in what foreign observers correctly read as factional warfare — we give comfort to those who argue that self-government is simply too turbulent to be trusted.

We cannot win that argument by proving them right.

Stable, effective governance does not mean government free from criticism. It does not mean officials insulated from accountability. It means a system of laws and institutions that operate consistently enough — predictably enough — that citizens can trust them, that international partners can rely on them, that the slow, difficult work of democratic governance can actually be performed.

Every escalation of the impeachment norm invites further escalation. Every majority that weaponizes the process makes it more likely that the next majority will use it more aggressively still. This is not a partisan prediction. It is a structural certainty. Norms, once broken, do not repair themselves. They require deliberate, principled reconstruction.

That reconstruction is what I am calling for today.

Conclusion: The Republic Demands Better of Us

I close with this.

The men who built this Republic were imperfect men operating with imperfect information in a world they could not fully predict. But they gave us something extraordinary: a framework designed not for the best of us, but resilient enough to survive the worst of us. They built in safeguards. They built in friction. They built in deliberate inefficiencies because they understood that speed and passion are democracy's enemies when they are not disciplined by law and principle.

We have been spending down that capital for decades. We have been borrowing against the institutional trust they built, assuming it was inexhaustible, assuming that each escalation would be the last, assuming that our side's abuse of the mechanism was justified because theirs was worse.

It was never inexhaustible. The account is running low. And the only way to refill it is to do the hard, unpopular, deeply necessary work of restraining ourselves — of saying, with conviction, that the power to remove a duly elected official is too grave, too consequential, too foundational to be wielded casually by whichever faction happens to hold a majority on any particular Tuesday.

That is not weakness. That is constitutional maturity.

That is the Republic our Founders built.

That is the Republic we owe our children.

Raise the standards. Restore the gravity. Return the process to its proper, solemn, extraordinary purpose.

And let us prove — once more, to ourselves and to the watching world — that we are still capable of governing ourselves.

Thank you.

The constitutional provisions for impeachment and removal of federal officials, particularly the President, were designed in an era when the Framers sought a balanced mechanism strong enough to uphold the rule of law yet restrained enough to prevent easy factional overthrow. Over the past two generations, impeachment has devolved into a routine instrument of partisan combat rather than an extraordinary remedy of last resort. Lowering confidence in the original high threshold of “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors” has produced serial House inquiries that command diminished public support, distract government from urgent governance, and erode the stability the Constitution intended. Raising the required threshold for removal from the current two-thirds Senate supermajority to something materially higher—four-fifths or, more functionally, requiring simultaneous concurrence of both houses at their current majorities while leaving the hearing process intact—would sharply curtail politicization while preserving accountability.

The present two-thirds Senate threshold has proven inadequate to deter partisan impeachment because the political cost of bringing articles in the House is essentially zero whenever one party commands a majority. Modern impeachment inquiries routinely open with little or no bipartisan support; they function less as deliberative trials than as messaging operations whose principal audience is the next electoral calendar. Each cycle normalizes the practice: new allegations are pressed, procedural shortcuts are taken, and public discourse fractures along party lines regardless of the substantive merits. Raising the removal threshold forces potential impeachers to anticipate failure from the outset. When the only conceivable outcome is acquittal, partisan actors gain less from launching the inquiry, reducing the incentive to weaponize process against opponents outright. The lowered political return simultaneously disciplines the House, encouraging narrower, more evidence-driven resolutions before that body commits its limited prestige to a doomed effort.

Constitutional history supports elevating the bar. The phrase “high Crimes and Misdemeanors” was understood by the Framers to encompass serious abuses of power rather than policy disagreements or private misconduct. Hamilton in Federalist No. 65 warned that impeachment “will seldom fail to agitate the passions of the whole community,” anticipating exactly the factional turbulence later observed. Elevating the required removal vote aligns institutional incentives with this original vision by making conviction rarer and therefore more solemn. It does not eliminate investigation; House committees would retain full power to investigate, subpoena, and refer, preserving the informational and deterrent functions impeachment serves. It does, however, relegate removal to true emergencies where an official’s continuing tenure demonstrably threatens constitutional order rather than merely inconveniencing the opposition.

Empirical patterns in recent decades illustrate the risks of the current threshold. Both the 1998 and 2019 impeachments moved forward despite the acknowledged improbability of securing two-thirds Senate support; both produced near-perfect party-line voting and negligible long-term public shift. The lesson drawn by political actors is straightforward: the mere holding of impeachment hearings confers narrative advantage and base mobilization at negligible cost. Raising removal difficulty breaks this calculation by converting impeachment from a low-risk partisan ritual into a costlier institutional decision that no single party can credibly threaten on its own. Stability is thereby restored to the executive branch, allowing presidents to serve full terms unless egregious conduct unites an overwhelming cross-partisan majority.

Critics may object that a higher threshold entrenches misbehavior or renders removal impossibly remote. Yet the historical record shows that successful removals of presidents have never occurred even under the current rule, while cabinet and judicial officials have been removed through lower political costs and, in the case of judges, lifetime tenure itself supplies stronger incentives for caution. The proposed elevation does not abolish removal; it merely enforces the original constitutional presumption that removal should be extraordinary. Judicial review and elections remain available for lesser grievances. If evidence of criminality surfaces, the ordinary criminal justice system—complete with prosecutorial independence, plea bargaining, and jury trials—can address personal misconduct without transforming Congress into a substitute tribunal.

A significantly higher threshold would also improve public perception of constitutional legitimacy. At present, each successive impeachment erodes public trust because observers correctly perceive partisan motivations. Requiring four-fifths Senate support or equivalent dual-house concurrence would demand demonstrable, cross-cutting consensus before an elected President can be removed mid-term. Institutional resilience, not partisan convenience, is the proper constitutional lodestar.

Impeachment in the U.S. Constitution sets a deliberately high bar under Article II, Section 4: federal officials (primarily the President, Vice President, and civil officers) may be removed only for “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.” The House has the sole power of impeachment by simple majority; the Senate tries the case and convicts only with a two-thirds vote of members present. They embed structural safeguards against easy removal, reflecting the Framers’ emphasis on governmental stability, insulation from transient partisanship, and executive independence.

Core Design Principles from the Constitutional Convention

  • Stability and continuity of the executive branch. Frequent or low-threshold removals would expose the presidency to short-term political majorities, disrupt administration of the laws, and risk turning regular electoral competition into serial removal battles. The two-thirds Senate requirement is explicitly supermajoritarian to prevent one faction from ousting the executive without broad cross-party consensus.
  • Protection against partisan or factional abuse. James Madison and others warned that lowering the removal standard or process would invite “the mere will of a majority” or “the most corrupt and oppressive” majorities to displace officers. Historical experience with state constitutions and parliamentary systems informed the choice of a high barrier rather than simple-majority votes or legislative supremacy over the executive.
  • Separation of powers and checks. Impeachment serves as a narrow exception to fixed terms and electoral accountability; the high bar prevents Congress from converting it into a general oversight or veto power over the executive. Requiring concurrence of both chambers under distinct voting rules forces deliberation and coalition-building across political divides.

Policy Rationale for Maintaining or Increasing Thresholds

Arguments that favor preserving the constitutional supermajority or further raising procedural hurdles rest on empirical patterns of use and risks of lowered standards:

  1. Deterring weaponization along partisan lines. In a polarized environment with narrow congressional majorities possible, a simple-majority House vote already allows one chamber to initiate formally. Lowering the Senate threshold (or converting it to present-and-voting majorities) would make successful removal mainly a function of partisan arithmetic rather than sustained evidence of disqualifying conduct. Proposals to raise thresholds—for example, requiring a supermajority in the House to impeach or three-quarters in the Senate—aim to ensure even greater cross-aisle agreement, reducing the incentive for symbolic or retaliatory articles.

  2. Preserving democratic legitimacy and fixed terms. The presidency is chosen by a national electoral process (filtered through the Electoral College) for a fixed term. Easy impeachment effectively substitutes legislative judgment for that verdict. Higher barriers reinforce that elections, not Congress, determine the executive’s tenure absent extraordinary misconduct. This aligns with republican theory that separation of powers and fixed terms protect against legislative aggrandizement.

  3. Reducing institutional disruption and gridlock. Removal triggers succession (Vice President to the presidency), new confirmations, and potential policy discontinuity. Each instance consumes legislative time, media focus, and public attention. Historical data show most impeachments have not produced convictions; multiple failed or narrowly partisan attempts illustrate how low bars can produce protracted contests that weaken perceived legitimacy without achieving removal. Raising procedural costs (longer notice periods, mandatory factual findings committees, or higher evidentiary thresholds) discourages marginal filings.

  4. Safeguarding against public and international perception of instability. Repeated impeachment efforts, especially along party lines, have historically been criticized as undermining confidence in government continuity. Comparative examples—such as more fluid parliamentary confidence votes or recall mechanisms in some states—demonstrate faster turnover but also more frequent leadership churn. Higher federal barriers maintain executive capacity to conduct diplomacy, command armed forces, and execute statutes without constant threat of displacement.

  5. Distinguishing impeachment from ordinary accountability mechanisms. Ordinary policy disagreement, poor performance, or unpopular decisions remain addressable through elections, congressional oversight, funding controls, and judicial review. Impeachment is reserved for abuse of office; elevating thresholds or adding layers (e.g., required independent fact-finding commissions before House vote) further clarifies this distinction and protects officials from conflation with partisan performance reviews.

Empirical observations about low historical conviction rates (Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton, Donald Trump’s first trial) are often cited as evidence that the system already functions to protect against casual removal, yet critics argue narrow majorities still initiate proceedings for signaling purposes. Proponents of reinforcement therefore view modest increases in required votes or added procedural steps as insurance against erosion of the original constitutional equilibrium.

These considerations favor greater institutional inertia: a presidency that cannot be lightly overturned maintains the capacity for long-term policy execution, resists factional clamor, and channels accountability primarily through periodic elections rather than perpetual legislative trials.

Executive and judicial officers may plan and act with the knowledge that removal remains a remote constitutional remedy rather than an ordinary political hazard. Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of making the impeachment process for federal officials in the United States significantly more difficult by raising the constitutional threshold required for removal from office, in order to reduce politicization and protect against partisan misuse.
Model Response:

The Case for Raising the Bar: Why Impeachment Should Be Harder

Introduction

The framers of the United States Constitution regarded impeachment as a remedy of last resort — a constitutional emergency brake to be pulled only when the Republic faced a genuine crisis of governance. Yet in recent decades, the impeachment process has drifted from its intended purpose. What was conceived as a rare, solemn constitutional mechanism has increasingly become a tactical instrument of partisan warfare, deployed not to address clear abuses of power but to wound political opponents and energize electoral bases. This degradation of impeachment threatens the stability of American self-governance and calls for a serious reconsideration of whether the current constitutional threshold adequately protects against misuse.

This essay argues that the impeachment process should be made significantly more difficult — not to shield corrupt officials from accountability, but to preserve impeachment's extraordinary character and protect democratic governance from the corrosive effects of weaponized constitutional mechanisms.

I. The Framers' Design and Its Erosion

The Constitution specifies that federal officials may be removed from office upon conviction by two-thirds of the Senate for "Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors." The framers deliberately set a high bar. Alexander Hamilton, writing in Federalist No. 65, described impeachable offenses as those that relate "chiefly to injuries done immediately to the society itself" — violations so serious that they threaten the constitutional order itself, not merely policy disagreements or political failings.

Hamilton also recognized the inherent danger: that impeachment could become a tool of faction. He warned that the process would "connect itself with the pre-existing factions" and that partisan passions could distort judgment. The high threshold of a two-thirds Senate vote was intended as a safeguard against exactly this danger.

Yet the historical record reveals a troubling pattern of declining seriousness. The first presidential impeachment — Andrew Johnson in 1868 — was widely recognized even at the time as a political vendetta rooted in policy disagreement over Reconstruction. Johnson survived by a single vote, but the episode revealed how easily impeachment could be mobilized against an unpopular president for reasons far removed from constitutional crisis. More recently, the impeachments of Bill Clinton in 1998, Donald Trump in 2019 and 2021, and the near-constant threats of impeachment directed at presidents of both parties have further eroded the sense that impeachment is reserved for genuine emergencies.

Each of these episodes split almost entirely along partisan lines, regardless of the substantive merits. The pattern suggests that the current threshold — while nominally high — does not adequately prevent partisan mobilization around impeachment as a political tactic.

II. The Costs of Weaponized Impeachment

The politicization of impeachment carries real and serious costs that extend far beyond any single administration.

First, it destabilizes governance. The threat of impeachment creates a permanent atmosphere of constitutional crisis. When one party controls the House and the other holds the presidency, the temptation to deploy impeachment as a tool of opposition governance becomes nearly irresistible. This constant threat diverts political energy, institutional resources, and public attention from the substantive challenges of legislation and administration. It transforms the normal give-and-take of democratic politics into an existential struggle, encouraging maximalist rather than compromising behavior.

Second, it degrades the seriousness of the constitutional mechanism itself. If impeachment becomes routine — if it is deployed in every period of divided government — then it loses its gravity. Like a nuclear deterrent that is constantly threatened, its power diminishes with each empty invocation. When a genuine constitutional crisis eventually arises — when an official commits acts that truly warrant removal — the public may have become so inured to impeachment rhetoric that they cannot distinguish the extraordinary case from the ordinary partisan noise.

Third, it accelerates democratic erosion. Scholars of democratic decline consistently identify the weaponization of constitutional mechanisms as a key feature of democratic backsliding. When institutions designed to protect constitutional order are instead used as instruments of partisan combat, trust in those institutions — and in the constitutional system broadly — erodes. Citizens on the losing side of a partisan impeachment come to view the process as illegitimate, deepening polarization and weakening the shared commitment to constitutional governance that democratic stability requires.

Fourth, it creates perverse incentives for officials. When presidents know that impeachment is a routine partisan possibility rather than an extraordinary constitutional event, the incentive structure shifts. Officials may become more focused on maintaining partisan loyalty as a shield against potential impeachment than on governing well or upholding their constitutional obligations. The impeachment sword hanging permanently overhead encourages the very factionalism the framers sought to prevent.

III. The Proposal: Raising the Constitutional Threshold

To address these pathologies, the threshold for removal should be raised through constitutional amendment. Several specific reforms deserve consideration:

Requiring a supermajority of the House for impeachment articles. Currently, a simple majority of the House can impeach, which in practice means the majority party alone can initiate the process. Requiring a two-thirds vote (or another elevated threshold, such as three-fifths) to pass articles of impeachment would force genuine bipartisan consensus before the extraordinary step of removing an elected official from office. This change alone would transform impeachment from a partisan weapon into a genuine constitutional mechanism, ensuring that only actions commanding broad cross-party support could trigger the process.

Raising the Senate conviction threshold beyond two-thirds. While the current two-thirds requirement is already substantial, historical experience suggests it is not sufficient to prevent highly partisan impeachment proceedings. Raising the bar to, say, three-quarters of the Senate would make conviction practically impossible without overwhelming bipartisan agreement, ensuring that only the most clearly egregious abuses of power could result in removal.

Narrowing the definition of impeachable offenses. The phrase "high Crimes and Misdemeanors" has been interpreted with varying degrees of breadth throughout American history. A constitutional amendment could more precisely define the offenses warranting removal, limiting impeachment to acts of treason, bribery, deliberate subversion of constitutional processes, or other conduct that poses a clear and present danger to the constitutional order. This would foreclose the use of impeachment against officials for policy disagreements, personal conduct, or political miscalculations — matters that the electoral process is better suited to address.

Requiring a finding of fact by an independent body. Before articles of impeachment could be voted on, a bipartisan commission or judicial body could be required to make a preliminary finding that the alleged conduct, if proven, would constitute a constitutionally defined impeachable offense. This gatekeeping function would filter out frivolous or purely political impeachment efforts before they consume legislative time and public attention.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments

Critics of raising the impeachment threshold will raise several important objections, each of which deserves a serious response.

"This would make it impossible to hold corrupt officials accountable." This objection rests on a false dichotomy between impeachment and accountability. Impeachment is not the only — and should not be the primary — mechanism for addressing official misconduct. The American constitutional system contains numerous accountability mechanisms: elections, judicial review, legislative oversight, statutory criminal prosecution, inspector general investigations, and the Twenty-Fifth Amendment for presidential incapacity. Raising the impeachment bar would channel accountability concerns into these alternative mechanisms, which are better designed for routine oversight. Impeachment should be reserved for cases so serious that these ordinary mechanisms are inadequate — precisely the cases that would command the broad bipartisan support required under a higher threshold.

"This would embower rogue officials." To the contrary, making impeachment harder would make it more credible — and therefore more powerful. A process that requires genuine bipartisan consensus carries far greater moral and political weight than one that can be triggered by a bare partisan majority. An impeachment that commands three-quarters of the Senate would send an unmistakable signal to the nation and the world about the seriousness of the official's conduct. The rogue official who fears a bipartisan consensus for removal has more to fear, not less, than one who merely needs to worry about the opposing party.

"The current system works well enough." This argument is difficult to sustain given the historical record. The United States has now experienced multiple impeachments or near-impeachments that were driven primarily by partisan motivation rather than genuine constitutional crisis. The Clinton impeachment was widely perceived as partisan overreach; the Trump impeachments split almost entirely along party lines, with each side viewing the other's position as evidence of bad faith. If the current threshold is sufficient to prevent politicization, the evidence suggests otherwise.

"This is a partisan proposal designed to protect a particular political faction." This objection misunderstands the nature of constitutional design. Constitutional provisions should be evaluated not by their short-term partisan effects but by their long-term institutional consequences. A higher impeachment threshold would constrain all parties equally. The party that benefits from low thresholds today may find itself victimized by those same thresholds tomorrow, as the political pendulum inevitably swings. Sound constitutional design protects against the misuse of power regardless of which faction currently wields it.

V. Impeachment as Constitutional Emergency Medicine

The most compelling argument for raising the impeachment threshold rests on a simple metaphor: impeachment is constitutional emergency medicine, and the emergency room is not where you go for a routine checkup.

When emergency medicine is overused, two things happen. First, the emergency room becomes overwhelmed, unable to focus its resources on genuine life-threatening cases. Second, patients with minor ailments learn to game the system, consuming resources that should be reserved for critical cases. The same dynamic applies to impeachment. When the mechanism is routinely invoked for political purposes, it cannot perform its constitutional function when truly needed. And politicians learn that impeachment threats and proceedings are effective political tools, creating incentives for further abuse.

Raising the threshold forces political actors to triage — to distinguish between conduct that is merely objectionable and conduct that is constitutionally catastrophic. This is precisely the kind of disciplined judgment the framers envisioned. They did not design impeachment as a general-purpose tool for punishing officials who are doing a bad job, making unpopular decisions, or even committing lesser offenses. They designed it as a last resort for when the constitutional order itself is at risk.

Making impeachment harder does not mean making government less accountable. It means making the right kind of accountability — the kind that flows from elections, from legislative oversight, from judicial review, and from the rule of law — the primary mechanism by which citizens hold their leaders responsible. It preserves impeachment for the cases that truly matter: the cases where an official's conduct is so far beyond the bounds of acceptable governance that only removal from office can protect the Republic.

VI. The Deeper Principle: Constitutional Resilience

At its core, this argument is about constitutional resilience — the ability of a constitutional system to withstand the pressures of partisan conflict without collapsing into dysfunction or authoritarianism.

Constitutions endure not because they prevent conflict, but because they channel conflict into productive forms. Elections channel the competition for power into peaceful, periodic contests. Separation of powers channels ambition against ambition. Federalism distributes authority to prevent its concentration. Each of these mechanisms works because it imposes structure on conflict, forcing compromise and preventing any single faction from dominating.

Impeachment, as currently structured, fails this test. It imposes insufficient structure on the most dangerous form of political conflict — the conflict over whether an elected official should be removed before the end of their term. By requiring only a simple House majority to initiate and a two-thirds Senate vote to convict, the current framework makes impeachment too easy to weaponize and too hard to deploy legitimately.

Raising the threshold restores impeachment to its proper place in the constitutional architecture: a mechanism so difficult to invoke that it is used only when the stakes are truly existential, commanding a consensus so broad that it transcends ordinary partisan division. This is not a radical proposal. It is a restoration of the framers' original intent, adapted for a political environment more polarized and more prone to institutional abuse than anything Hamilton or Madison could have imagined.

Conclusion

The impeachment power is one of the most extraordinary grants of authority in any constitutional system — the power of one branch of government to remove a member of another. The framers understood its dangers and attempted to guard against them. But the guardrails they erected have proven insufficient against the pressures of modern partisan politics.

Making impeachment significantly harder — through higher voting thresholds, clearer definitions of impeachable conduct, and institutional gatekeeping — would protect democratic governance from the corrosive effects of weaponized constitutional mechanisms. It would restore impeachment to its proper role as a last resort for genuine constitutional crises, strengthen alternative accountability mechanisms, and reduce the incentives for partisan abuse.

This is not a proposal born of naivety about the reality of political power. It is a proposal born of the conviction that constitutional systems survive not because they trust politicians to exercise extraordinary powers wisely, but because they make the misuse of those powers structurally difficult. The goal is not to make government unaccountable, but to ensure that accountability operates through mechanisms designed for ordinary governance, while reserving the extraordinary mechanism of impeachment for the extraordinary cases that justify its use.

The Republic would be stronger for it.

Arguments for Higher Impeachment Thresholds

This is a genuine constitutional design question that scholars across the political spectrum have debated since the founding. Here are the principal arguments for maintaining or increasing procedural barriers:

Structural and Constitutional Arguments

The Framers' intent The constitutional convention deliberately chose supermajority requirements (two-thirds in the Senate for conviction) to prevent simple partisan majorities from removing officials. The Federalist Papers, particularly Hamilton in No. 65, argued impeachment proceedings were inherently susceptible to factional passions and that high barriers were necessary safeguards.

Separation of powers Lowering impeachment thresholds effectively shifts power toward the legislature, potentially allowing Congress to remove executive or judicial officials over policy disagreements rather than genuine misconduct. This could convert impeachment into a de facto vote of no confidence, fundamentally altering the presidential system's balance.

Judicial independence Federal judges serve life terms specifically to insulate them from political pressure. If impeachment becomes accessible to partisan majorities, judges may calculate decisions based on political survival rather than legal reasoning — undermining the judiciary's core function.

Stability and Governance Arguments

Functional continuity of government Frequent impeachments create institutional disruption, diverting enormous legislative resources and public attention from governance. Officials facing constant removal threats may struggle to make long-term policy decisions or engage in necessary negotiations.

The chilling effect on decision-making If removal becomes politically feasible over controversial but lawful decisions, officials may default to risk-averse positions that avoid accountability but also avoid difficult necessary choices — what political scientists call "governance by fear."

Precedent escalation Each use of impeachment normalizes its further use. Historically, impeachment frequency has escalated: from roughly once per century in the early republic to multiple proceedings in recent decades. Higher thresholds act as a brake on this normalization cycle.

Democratic Theory Arguments

Elections as the primary accountability mechanism In democratic systems, the electorate is the principal check on officeholders. Impeachment was designed as an extraordinary remedy for extraordinary misconduct — not routine political opposition. Critics argue that if voters can remove officials through elections, removing them through other means should require extraordinary consensus.

Minority protection of elected mandates If a simple legislative majority can remove executive officials, this effectively nullifies the electoral choices of voters who selected that official. Supermajority requirements protect the democratic legitimacy of elected mandates against narrow factional opposition.

Consensus as a proxy for genuine misconduct A high threshold forces the opposing party to persuade some members of the official's own party — creating a rough test that distinguishes genuine unfitness from partisan disagreement. This cross-partisan requirement suggests the conduct is serious enough to transcend ordinary politics.

Practical and Historical Considerations

Reducing strategic weaponization Lower thresholds invite what scholars call "impeachment as harassment" — proceedings initiated not to remove officials but to damage them politically, consume their administration's bandwidth, or energize a political base. Higher barriers raise the cost of strategic but insincere proceedings.

Protecting transitional periods Officials near the end of terms, or in lame-duck periods, become especially vulnerable to symbolic impeachments with no practical purpose. Higher thresholds reduce these purely performative exercises.

Important Counterpoints to Acknowledge

Scholars who favor maintaining current or higher thresholds generally still acknowledge several tensions:

  • Accountability concerns: Excessively high barriers can leave genuinely unfit officials in place, causing real harm
  • The abuse-of-power paradox: If barriers are too high, the threat of impeachment becomes hollow, reducing its deterrent effect
  • Context dependence: Some argue the appropriate threshold depends on the specific office (e.g., judges vs. presidents) and the specific nature of the alleged misconduct
  • Changing political norms: Defenders of existing or lower thresholds argue that current polarization makes impeachment more necessary, not less

This remains an active area of constitutional scholarship, with reasonable people disagreeing about where the optimal balance between accountability and stability lies. The tradeoffs are genuine — every increase in stability potentially reduces accountability, and vice versa.

Strengthening Impeachment: A Constitutional Safeguard Against Partisan Abuse

The impeachment power, envisioned by the framers as a crucial check against executive tyranny, has increasingly become a weapon of political warfare rather than a measured constitutional safeguard. The solution is not to abandon this vital tool, but to strengthen it by significantly raising the constitutional threshold required for removal from office. Making impeachment more difficult would restore its intended purpose as a truly exceptional remedy, protecting democratic institutions from the corrosive effects of partisan manipulation.

The Crisis of Impeachment Normalization

Since 1998, the United States has experienced impeachment proceedings against two presidents within a quarter-century—unprecedented in our nation's history. This acceleration reveals a dangerous trajectory where impeachment has evolved from an extraordinary constitutional remedy into a routine political tactic. The normalization of impeachment threatens the stability of our democratic institutions, creating a perpetual state of constitutional crisis that undermines public confidence and governmental effectiveness.

The framers explicitly designed impeachment to address only the most serious offenses—"high crimes and misdemeanors"—not ordinary political disagreements or policy disputes. Yet contemporary impeachments have blurred these distinctions, transforming what should be a grave constitutional moment into partisan theater. Raising the removal threshold would restore the deliberative gravity that the process demands.

The Case for Super-Majoritarian Requirements

Currently, conviction in the Senate requires only a two-thirds majority—a threshold that may seem high but has proven susceptible to partisan calculations. Consider implementing a three-fourths requirement for removal, perhaps with additional provisions such as state legislative approval or Supreme Court review of procedural matters. This would transform impeachment from a legislative-majority tool into a genuinely national consensus requirement.

Such heightened standards would serve multiple protective functions. First, they would ensure that only truly egregious misconduct—conduct that shocks the conscience of the entire political spectrum—could justify removal. Second, they would force bipartisan agreement on the severity of offenses, reducing the likelihood that legitimate policy differences morph into impeachable claims. Third, they would create space for investigation, deliberation, and potential resolution through normal democratic processes, including elections.

Protecting Legitimate Governance

When impeachment becomes too easily invoked, it paralyzes legitimate governance. Officials operate under constant threat of removal for actions that fall within normal political discourse. This chilling effect undermines effective administration and prevents leaders from making difficult but necessary decisions. A more stringent impeachment process would provide officials with greater security to govern boldly while maintaining appropriate accountability.

The current system also encourages strategic behavior: members of Congress calibrate their actions based on impeachment potential rather than pure policy considerations. This distortion of incentives degrades the quality of legislation and executive decision-making. Heightened impeachment barriers would allow political actors to focus on substantive governance rather than constitutional brinkmanship.

Historical Precedent and Constitutional Wisdom

The founders themselves worried extensively about impeachment's potential for abuse. Alexander Hamilton warned that impeachment trials might become "the favorite weapon of the seditious" and advocated for procedures that would ensure careful deliberation. James Madison emphasized that impeachment should address only the most serious threats to republican government.

Throughout American history, the most successful impeachments—such as those of federal judges like Samuel Chase and West H. Humphreys—involved clear evidence of corruption and universally condemned behavior. These cases succeeded partly because they commanded broad consensus rather than narrow partisan support.

Practical Implementation Strategies

Several constitutional amendments could achieve the desired effect. One approach would require conviction by three-fourths of senators present, with a minimum participation rate to prevent quorum manipulation. Another might mandate that removal decisions receive affirmative votes in both houses representing states that collectively comprise a supermajority of the national population, ensuring geographic legitimacy alongside numerical support.

Additionally, incorporating judicial review of impeachment procedures or requiring pre-removal Supreme Court certification of evidentiary standards could add layers of institutional protection. These modifications would not eliminate impeachment's deterrent effect but would ensure its application only under genuinely exceptional circumstances.

Addressing Counterarguments

Critics might argue that making impeachment more difficult would immunize genuinely corrupt officials from accountability. However, this concern misunderstands the proper relationship between impeachment and ordinary legal processes. Criminal prosecution, civil litigation, and electoral accountability remain available for addressing official misconduct that falls short of constitutional removal standards.

Moreover, the threat of enhanced impeachment scrutiny can actually improve official behavior. When officials know that removal requires extraordinary consensus, they have stronger incentives to maintain broadly acceptable conduct rather than narrowly avoiding partisan condemnation.

Conclusion

The impeachment power represents one of democracy's most solemn responsibilities—the authority to remove officials who threaten constitutional order. Yet this power becomes dangerous when too easily exercised, transforming from protection against tyranny into a tool of partisan advantage. By raising constitutional thresholds for removal, we can restore impeachment's proper role as an exceptional safeguard while preserving its deterrent effect against genuine abuses of power.

Such reforms would signal a renewed commitment to principled governance over political opportunism, protecting both democratic institutions and individual officials from the arbitrary exercise of impeachment power. In strengthening the barriers to removal, we ultimately strengthen democracy itself.

But in an age of intense polarization, that line is increasingly blurred. Every major controversy is framed as an existential threat; every constitutional clash is described as unprecedented; every opponent is portrayed not merely as mistaken, but illegitimate.     • Supposed Benefit: By making impeachment initiation or conviction harder, the focus would arguably remain sharper on instances of truly severe constitutional breaches or corruption, ensuring that the ultimate sanction of removal from office is reserved for the most egregious offenses rather than becoming a routine feature of partisan conflict or a tool used for policy change that cannot be achieved through legislation.

  5. Reducing Extreme Polarization and Gridlock:

    • Reason: The threat and actual use of impeachment have become flashpoints for extreme political rhetoric and partisanship. Knowing that removal might be even more difficult could shift the focus away from purely symbolic or potentially politically-motivated impeachment votes towards negotiations, oversight, and accountability measures short of removal.

Important Considerations:

  • Constitutionality: Modifying the voting threshold for either House approval of articles of impeachment or Senate conviction would likely require a constitutional amendment, as the Constitution implicitly defines the process based on existing legislative rules and sets the Senate as the tribunal.
  • Procedural Changes: It's possible for the House or Senate to change their own internal rules (like the House Rules Committee requirements for bringing forward articles, or House ethics committee procedures) without a constitutional amendment, potentially increasing the procedural hurdles.
  • Potential Downsides: Critics argue that making impeachment harder could allow officials guilty of serious misconduct but failing to achieve a supermajority consensus to remain in office. It could also weaken a crucial check on executive and judicial power, arguably moving the balance of power further towards elected officials accountable mainly at the next election cycle.

In summary, the argument for increasing the difficulty of impeachment is fundamentally driven by a concern that the current low procedural barriers allow for too much political opportunism and partisanship in what was intended to be a serious constitutional remedy. The purported benefits revolve around increasing governmental stability, ensuring a broader consensus is required before invoking such a severe penalty, and preserving impeachment primarily for instances of severely damaging constitutional misconduct.
